title: UNIT 3: PHYSICAL STATES OF MATTER
notes:
✓ Matter → Anything that has mass and occupies space.

◆ COMMON PHYSICAL STATES
✓ Solid.
✓ Liquid.
✓ Gas.
✓ Plasma → A physical state that occurs under extremely high-energy conditions.

→ The physical state of a substance depends mainly on particle motion, intermolecular attractions, temperature, and pressure.
→ Changes in temperature and/or pressure can cause changes from one state to another.

title: 3.1 Introduction
notes:
✓ Matter exists mainly as solids, liquids, and gases.
✓ Water → Ice is the solid state, water is the liquid state, and steam is the gaseous state.

✓ Solids and liquids → Condensed states because their particles are relatively close together and their densities are much greater than those of gases.
✓ Liquids and gases → Fluids because they can flow.

→ A substance can change from one physical state to another by changing temperature and/or pressure.

◆ COMMON CHANGES OF STATE
✓ Melting.
✓ Freezing.
✓ Vaporization.
✓ Condensation.
✓ Sublimation.
✓ Deposition.

title: 3.1.1 States of Matter
notes:
◆ SOLID
✓ A solid has a definite shape and definite volume.
✓ Its particles are closely packed and highly organized.
→ Particles mainly vibrate about fixed positions, so solids are rigid and nearly incompressible.

◆ LIQUID
✓ A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape.
→ It takes the shape of its container and can flow.
✓ Its particles remain relatively close together but can move past one another.

◆ GAS
✓ A gas has neither definite shape nor definite volume.
→ It fills its container and is highly compressible because there is considerable empty space between particles.

◆ PLASMA
✓ Plasma → An ionized gas containing positive ions and electrons.
→ It occurs at extremely high temperatures and, like a gas, has no definite shape or volume.

title: 3.2 Kinetic Theory and Properties of Matter
notes:
✓ Kinetic theory → Explains the physical states of matter in terms of the motion, energy, spacing, and attractive forces of particles.

✓ Particles of matter → Are continuously moving.
✓ Average kinetic energy → Increases as temperature increases.

→ Solid → Least particle motion.
→ Liquid → Greater particle motion.
→ Gas → Greatest particle motion.

→ The spaces between particles become progressively larger from solid to liquid to gas.
✓ Intermolecular forces → Attractive forces between particles that become more important when particles are close together.

title: 3.2.1 The Kinetic Theory of Matter
notes:
✓ The kinetic theory of matter is based on these main ideas:
◆ All matter consists of very small particles such as atoms, molecules, or ions.
◆ Particles are in continuous and random motion.
◆ Particles possess kinetic and potential energy.
◆ Gas particles have greater average energy and freedom of movement than liquid and solid particles.
◆ Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of particles.
◆ There are spaces between particles, and these spaces generally increase from solid to liquid to gas.
◆ Attractive forces exist between particles and become stronger as particles move closer together.

→ A change in the energy of particles can cause a change in physical state.

title: 3.2.2 Properties of Matter
notes:
✓ The properties of each state can be explained using particle arrangement and motion.

◆ SOLIDS
✓ Fixed shape and volume.
✓ High organization.
✓ Very limited particle movement.

◆ LIQUIDS
✓ Fixed volume but variable shape.
✓ Particles are close together but have enough freedom to flow.

◆ GASES
✓ Variable shape and volume.
✓ Low density.
✓ Large spaces between particles.
✓ High compressibility.

◆ PLASMA
✓ Consists mainly of positive ions and free electrons.
→ Behaves similarly to a gas in having no fixed shape or volume.

title: 3.3 The Gaseous State
notes:
✓ Gases → Consist of particles that are widely separated and move rapidly in random directions.

→ Large empty spaces make gases highly compressible and allow them to expand and mix easily.

✓ Gas pressure → Results from collisions of gas particles with the walls of their container.

◆ IMPORTANT GAS VARIABLES
✓ Pressure (P).
✓ Volume (V).
✓ Temperature (T).
✓ Amount of gas in moles (n).

→ Gas behavior is described by several gas laws relating these variables.

title: 3.3.1 The Kinetic Molecular Theory of Gases
notes:
✓ The kinetic molecular theory of gases assumes that:
◆ A gas consists of very small particles in continuous straight-line motion.
◆ Gas particles are separated by large spaces compared with their sizes.
◆ The volume of individual particles is negligible compared with the total gas volume.
◆ There are negligible attractive or repulsive forces between ideal gas particles.
◆ Collisions between particles and container walls are elastic.
◆ The average kinetic energy of gas particles is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

✓ Kinetic energy of a particle:
KE = ½mv²

✓ m → Mass.
✓ v → Velocity.

→ Increasing temperature increases the average speed and kinetic energy of gas particles.

title: 3.3.2 The Gas Laws
notes:
✓ Gas laws → Describe how pressure, volume, temperature, and amount of gas are related.

◆ BOYLE’S LAW
✓ At constant temperature, the volume of a fixed amount of gas is inversely proportional to pressure.
✓ P₁V₁ = P₂V₂

◆ CHARLES’S LAW
✓ At constant pressure, the volume of a fixed amount of gas is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
✓ V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂

◆ GAY-LUSSAC’S LAW
✓ At constant volume, the pressure of a fixed amount of gas is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
✓ P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂

◆ COMBINED GAS LAW
✓ P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂

✓ Temperature must be expressed in kelvin for gas-law calculations.

title: 3.3.2.1 Avogadro’s Law
notes:
✓ Avogadro’s law → At constant temperature and pressure, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to the number of moles of gas.

✓ V ∝ n
✓ V₁/n₁ = V₂/n₂

→ Equal volumes of different gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

✓ Standard molar volume → Approximately 22.4 L mol⁻¹ at STP.
→ Approximately 1 mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 L at STP.

title: 3.3.2.2 Ideal Gas Equation
notes:
✓ Combining Boyle’s law, Charles’s law, and Avogadro’s law gives the ideal gas equation:
PV = nRT

✓ P → Pressure.
✓ V → Volume.
✓ n → Number of moles.
✓ R → Gas constant.
✓ T → Absolute temperature in kelvin.

→ The equation can be used to calculate an unknown pressure, volume, temperature, or amount of gas.

title: 3.3.2.3 Ideal and Real Gases
notes:
✓ Ideal gas → A theoretical gas whose particles have negligible volume, experience no intermolecular attractions, and undergo perfectly elastic collisions.

✓ Real gases → Do not behave perfectly according to the ideal-gas assumptions.
→ Their particles have finite volume and experience intermolecular attractions.

→ Real gases behave most nearly like ideal gases at relatively high temperatures and low pressures, where particles are farther apart and intermolecular attractions are less significant.

title: 3.3.2.4 Diffusion and Graham’s Law
notes:
✓ Diffusion → The spontaneous mixing or spreading of gas particles from a region of higher concentration toward a region of lower concentration due to their continuous random motion.

✓ Graham’s law → The rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass.

✓ r₁/r₂ = √(M₂/M₁)

→ Lighter gases diffuse faster than heavier gases under the same conditions.

✓ Rate of diffusion is also inversely related to the time required to travel a given distance:
r ∝ 1/t

title: 3.4 The Liquid State
notes:
✓ Liquids → Have definite volume but no definite shape.

→ Their particles are closer together than gas particles and experience stronger intermolecular attractions.

✓ Liquid particles → Are continuously moving, but their movement is more restricted than in gases.

◆ IMPORTANT INTERMOLECULAR FORCES
✓ Dipole–dipole forces.
✓ London dispersion forces.
✓ Hydrogen bonding.

→ Liquids are generally denser than gases and less dense than solids.
→ The strength of intermolecular attractions influences properties such as volatility, vapor pressure, and boiling point.

title: 3.4.1 Energy Changes in Liquids
notes:
→ When energy is supplied to a liquid, the kinetic energy of its particles increases.
→ Heating increases the temperature and vapor pressure of the liquid.

◆ VAPORIZATION
✓ Conversion of liquid to gas.
→ It can occur through evaporation or boiling.

◆ EVAPORATION
✓ Only particles at the liquid surface escape into the gas phase.
→ The most energetic surface particles are more likely to escape.
✓ Can occur below the boiling point.

◆ CONDENSATION
✓ Conversion of gas to liquid.
→ It occurs when vapor particles lose energy and return to the liquid.

→ In a closed container, evaporation and condensation can reach dynamic equilibrium.

title: 3.4.1.1 Vapor Pressure and Volatility
notes:
✓ Vapor pressure → The pressure exerted by a vapor when it is in dynamic equilibrium with its liquid at a particular temperature.

→ Vapor pressure increases as temperature increases because more particles have enough kinetic energy to escape from the liquid.

→ Stronger intermolecular attractions make it more difficult for particles to escape, resulting in lower vapor pressure.

✓ Volatile liquid → Evaporates easily and generally has relatively weak intermolecular attractions and high vapor pressure.
✓ Nonvolatile liquid → Evaporates less easily and generally has stronger attractions and lower vapor pressure.

title: 3.4.1.2 Boiling and Boiling Point
notes:
✓ Boiling → Occurs when vapor bubbles form throughout a liquid and can rise to the surface without collapsing.

✓ A liquid boils when its vapor pressure becomes equal to the external pressure.

✓ Normal boiling point → Temperature at which the vapor pressure of a liquid equals 1 atmosphere.

→ Increasing external pressure raises the boiling point, while decreasing external pressure lowers it.
→ At higher altitudes, where atmospheric pressure is lower, liquids generally boil at lower temperatures.

✓ During boiling of a pure liquid at constant pressure → Temperature remains constant until the liquid has completely changed into vapor.

title: 3.5 The Solid State
notes:
✓ Solids → Have definite shape and definite volume because their particles are closely packed and held by attractive forces.
→ Particles mainly vibrate around fixed positions.

◆ TYPES OF SOLIDS
✓ Crystalline solids.
✓ Amorphous solids.

◆ CRYSTALLINE SOLIDS
✓ Particles are arranged in an orderly repeating pattern.
✓ Generally have a definite melting point.

◆ AMORPHOUS SOLIDS
✓ Have no long-range regular arrangement.
✓ Generally soften over a range of temperatures.

→ Heating a solid increases particle motion. When enough energy is supplied, the ordered structure can be disrupted and the solid melts.

title: 3.5.1 Melting, Freezing and Fusion
notes:
✓ Melting or fusion → Conversion of a solid into a liquid.
✓ Melting point → Temperature at which a crystalline solid changes into a liquid.

✓ Freezing or solidification → Conversion of a liquid into a solid.
→ For a pure substance, the freezing point is the same temperature as its melting point under the same pressure.

✓ At the melting/freezing point → Solid and liquid can coexist in dynamic equilibrium.

→ Melting requires energy and is endothermic.
→ Freezing releases energy and is exothermic.

✓ Molar heat of fusion (ΔHfus) → Energy required to convert one mole of solid into liquid at its melting point.

✓ ΔHcryst = −ΔHfus

title: 3.5.2 Sublimation and Deposition
notes:
✓ Sublimation → Direct conversion of a solid into a gas without passing through the liquid state.
✓ Example → Iodine can sublime.

✓ Deposition → Direct conversion of a gas into a solid without passing through the liquid state.

→ Sublimation requires energy to overcome attractive forces and is endothermic.
→ Deposition releases energy and is exothermic.

✓ Enthalpy relationships:
ΔHsub = ΔHfus + ΔHvap
ΔHdep = −ΔHsub

title: 3.5.3 Heating Curve and Phase Changes
notes:
✓ Heating curve → Shows how the temperature of a substance changes as heat is supplied.

→ During a single phase, added heat generally increases the temperature because particle kinetic energy increases.

→ During a phase change, the temperature remains constant while the supplied energy is used mainly to overcome intermolecular attractions and change the arrangement of particles.

✓ Plateaus on a heating curve → Represent phase changes such as melting and boiling.

◆ MAJOR PHASE CHANGES
✓ Fusion → Solid → Liquid → Energy absorbed.
✓ Vaporization → Liquid → Gas → Energy absorbed.
✓ Sublimation → Solid → Gas → Energy absorbed.
✓ Freezing → Liquid → Solid → Energy released.
✓ Condensation → Gas → Liquid → Energy released.
✓ Deposition → Gas → Solid → Energy released.

title: UNIT 3 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
✓ MATTER → Anything that has mass and occupies space.

✓ SOLID → Definite shape and volume; particles closely packed and mainly vibrating.
✓ LIQUID → Definite volume but no definite shape; particles can move past one another.
✓ GAS → No definite shape or volume; particles widely separated and highly mobile.
✓ PLASMA → Ionized gas containing positive ions and electrons.

✓ KINETIC THEORY → Matter consists of continuously moving particles with kinetic and potential energy.
✓ TEMPERATURE → Related to the average kinetic energy of particles.

✓ BOYLE’S LAW → P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
✓ CHARLES’S LAW → V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂.
✓ GAY-LUSSAC’S LAW → P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂.
✓ AVOGADRO’S LAW → V₁/n₁ = V₂/n₂.
✓ COMBINED GAS LAW → P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.
✓ IDEAL GAS LAW → PV = nRT.

✓ STANDARD MOLAR VOLUME → Approximately 22.4 L mol⁻¹ at STP.

✓ DIFFUSION → Spreading of gas particles due to random molecular motion.
✓ GRAHAM’S LAW → r₁/r₂ = √(M₂/M₁).

✓ EVAPORATION → Surface vaporization that can occur below the boiling point.
✓ CONDENSATION → Gas → Liquid.
✓ VAPOR PRESSURE → Pressure of vapor in equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature.
✓ BOILING → Vaporization throughout the liquid when vapor pressure equals external pressure.

✓ MELTING/FUSION → Solid → Liquid; energy absorbed.
✓ FREEZING/SOLIDIFICATION → Liquid → Solid; energy released.
✓ SUBLIMATION → Solid → Gas; energy absorbed.
✓ DEPOSITION → Gas → Solid; energy released.

✓ HEAT OF FUSION → Energy required to convert one mole of solid to liquid at its melting point.
✓ HEATING CURVE → Temperature increases within a phase, while temperature remains constant during a phase change.

→ KEY IDEA → The physical behavior of matter is determined by particle motion, particle spacing, kinetic energy, and intermolecular attractions.
